# Sam's News — conservation — 2026-09-26

## Conservation

### <span class="imp imp-high" title="Importance 8/10" aria-label="Importance 8 of 10">8</span> Trump Administration Removes Habitat Protections from Endangered Species Act
The president of the United States finalized a rule on July 10, 2026, removing the regulatory definition of "harm" from the Endangered Species Act, eliminating decades-old habitat protection for endangered wildlife. The change, effective September 14, 2026, allows habitat destruction to proceed without legal consequence as long as animals are not directly killed, fundamentally weakening endangered species protections across the nation.

<ul class="takeaways">
<li>Rule removes regulatory definition of &#x27;harm&#x27; to include habitat degradation, effective September 14, 2026</li>
<li>Habitat destruction no longer counts as illegal &#x27;take&#x27; under the Endangered Species Act</li>
<li>Change reverses 30+ years of legal interpretation upheld in 1995 Supreme Court decision (Babbitt v. Sweet Home)</li>
<li>Habitat loss is identified as the primary driver of extinction for endangered species</li>
<li>Farming, drilling, mining, logging, and development can now proceed in endangered species habitats without federal restriction</li>
</ul>

## Conservation Policy

### <span class="imp imp-high" title="Importance 7/10" aria-label="Importance 7 of 10">7</span> Trump administration endangered species rollbacks threaten Canadian wildlife conservation
The U.S. Department of the Interior repealed the decades-old definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act on July 10, 2026, taking effect September 14. The change weakens protections for habitat degradation, affecting migratory species that cross the U.S.-Canada border including spotted owls, grizzly bears, and killer whales.

<ul class="takeaways">
<li>Repealed ESA &quot;harm&quot; definition previously upheld by U.S. Supreme Court in mid-1990s</li>
<li>Takes effect September 14, 2026</li>
<li>Threatens transboundary species: migratory birds, northern spotted owls, grizzly bears, killer whales</li>
<li>Nearly a dozen groups filed lawsuit in U.S. District Court</li>
</ul>
